events.description: U.S.-Taliban withdrawal deal signed, with May 1, 2021 withdrawal date; hosts say it released thousands of Taliban prisoners and has no counterterrorism enforcement
Taliban English statement warning the U.S. not to renegotiate the Doha agreement or face all-out war
Deadline for U.S. withdrawal under the agreement; Taliban say attacks on U.S. forces will resume if troops remain
Rocket attack in Erbil wounded Americans and killed a contractor; another rocket attack hit the U.S. Embassy
UNAMA report on civilian casualties finds numbers down in 2020 but surging after peace talks started

relationships.quote: The Taliban and the Afghan government hadn't met for 35 days.

sources_cited: UNAMA civilian casualties report 'Surge in civilian casualties following Afghanistan peace negotiations start'
key_claims: There is no genuine peace process; the Feb 2020 deal is a withdrawal deal whose only concrete item is the May 1, 2021 U.S. exit date.
The Taliban has made no counterterrorism moves against al-Qaeda and refused to publicly renounce it.
If U.S. forces stay past May 1, the Taliban will resume attacks on U.S. forces and walk away from Doha talks.
The Taliban is trying to run out the clock, refusing a ceasefire and not meeting the Afghan government for 35 days.
Per UNAMA, the Taliban caused 45% of civilian casualties, and with ISKP over 50%, versus 22% for the Afghan government.
In Iraq there is no withdrawal deadline, but Iranian-backed militias threaten U.S. forces, creating tension with Biden's desire to rejoin the Iran nuclear deal.
The predominant thinking in the U.S. foreign policy establishment is to move on from post-9/11 conflicts, which includes a push to explain away and pretend that ISIS and al-Qaeda do not matter.
The hosts argue that the counterterrorism field is too dogmatic, with a long-standing drive to 'disconnect the dots' between jihadist groups.
The hosts urge President Biden to assess the actual facts and decision points on Afghanistan and Iraq rather than act on preconceptions.
